meta.blurb: History never repeats exactly, yet it keeps rhyming. Meet twelve patterns, from stretched empires to bursting bubbles, each shown through real people in Rome, Amsterdam, Paris and beyond. Learn what the past can and cannot tell us.
meta.bible: This book explains twelve patterns, called rules, with real examples; the rules are habits and tendencies, not laws, and exceptions are mentioned. Rome: the Roman Empire, at its greatest size around the year 117 under the Emperor Trajan, with Hadrian after him; Mesopotamia. Diocletian: Roman emperor, price edict of 301. Spain: silver from the Americas, crown debts. Germany: hyperinflation of 1923, Rentenmark introduced in November 1923, about four trillion marks to the dollar. Gutenberg: printing press around 1450 in Mainz. Martin Luther: Ninety-five Theses, 1517, Reformation. Catholic Church: list of banned books, 1559. Washington and Baltimore: first long-distance telegraph message, 1844; Atlantic cable 1858 and 1866. Dutch Republic: tulip bulbs, crash in early 1637, story probably exaggerated. South Sea Company: 1720, Isaac Newton said to have lost money. France: poor harvest of 1788, Louis XVI, Estates-General, the Bastille on 14 July 1789, Napoleon Bonaparte took power in 1799 and was crowned in 1804; Alexis de Tocqueville. Black Death: reached Messina in Sicily in October 1347; perhaps a third or more of Europe died, estimates uncertain; England, Statute of Labourers 1351, Peasants' Revolt 1381. Carthage: destroyed by Rome in 146 BC. Congress of Vienna: 1814 and 1815. Treaty of Versailles: 1919, reparations. Odoacer and Romulus Augustulus: 476. Constantinople: fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Venice: republic until 1797, the Arsenal. Silk Road: Samarkand and Kashgar. Vasco da Gama: reached India in 1498, Lisbon, Amsterdam. Britain: slave trade banned 1807, slavery abolished by an act of 1833. New Zealand: women won the vote in 1893; Switzerland 1971. Maginot Line: French forts of the 1930s; Ardennes, May 1940. Key words: Empire, Empires, Frontier, Inflation, Currency, Debts, Bubble, Reformation, Plague, Serfdom, Reparations, Archaeologists, Archives, Propaganda, Mediterranean, Atlantic. Voice: clear, curious and fair; careful about uncertainty; no invented numbers, quotes or studies.

Soldiers on far borders needed food, clothes, weapons and pay.
Spain was rich with silver in the 1500s, but it fought many wars.
Leaders often keep fighting because stopping feels like losing.

People stopped trusting the coins, and prices went up fast.
In Germany in 1923, money lost its value almost every day.
Money is trust, and trust is very hard to win back.
Rule three: new ways to share news shake the people in power.
In 1517, Martin Luther wrote his ideas, and printers spread them quickly.
In the 1800s, news could travel along wires in a few minutes.
Rulers try to control new tools, but they cannot stop everything.

Some historians think the flower story was not quite true.
In 1720, many English people bought shares in one company and lost money.
When everyone says this time is different, be careful.
Rule five: hungry people can bring down a government.
On 14 July 1789, a crowd in Paris attacked the Bastille.
Revolutions often come when people hope for more, not only when they are poor.
Then a general named Napoleon took power in France.

After the plague, there were fewer workers, so workers asked for more pay.
In 1381, English villagers marched against a new tax.

Rome destroyed the city of Carthage, so we hear Rome's side.

B1B2: People often say that history repeats itself, yet nobody has ever seen the same event happen twice. What does come back, again and again, are patterns.
The clothes and tools of people change, but their needs do not. In every age, people have felt fear, hunger, hope and pride, and these feelings drive much of what they do.
A pattern in history is a habit, not a law of nature. One example proves nothing, so we need many, and we must look for the exceptions as well.
Rule one is that empires tend to grow larger than they can safely guard. Around the year 117, Rome reached its greatest size, from Britain in the west to Mesopotamia in the east.
A long frontier needs soldiers, and soldiers need food, weapons and pay. The Roman army was paid in silver coins, so every new border made the empire's bills larger.

In the 1500s, Spain ruled huge lands and received great amounts of silver from its mines in the Americas. Even so, its wars across Europe cost so much that the crown several times declared itself unable to pay its debts.

Leaders rarely give up distant lands willingly, because retreat feels like defeat, and defeat can threaten their own power. So empires often keep spending on a frontier long after it has stopped paying for itself.
Rule two is that tricks with money end badly. Roman emperors who needed to pay their soldiers began mixing cheaper metal into the silver of their coins.
People soon noticed that the coins were worth less, so they asked for more of them. Prices rose, and in the year 301 the emperor Diocletian tried to fix maximum prices by law, which largely failed.
In Germany in 1923, prices rose so fast that people carried money in baskets and wheelbarrows. By November, one American dollar was worth about four trillion German marks.
Money works only as long as people believe that it will keep its value. In November 1923, Germany introduced a new currency, the Rentenmark, and together with other reforms it helped to calm prices.
Rule three is that new ways of sharing information shake the powerful. Around 1450, Gutenberg built a press in Mainz that made books much faster and cheaper.

In 1517, a monk named Martin Luther criticised some practices of the Church in his Ninety-five Theses. Printers copied his writings, and his ideas spread across Germany far faster than any scribe could have managed.

In 1844, the first long-distance electric telegraph message was sent in the United States, between Washington and Baltimore. Later, cables under the ocean joined Europe and America, so news that once took days arrived in minutes.

In 1559, the Church published a list of banned books, and many rulers licensed printers and censored the news. Yet each new tool brought lies and rumour as well as knowledge, and society needed time to adjust.
Rule four is that crowds can push prices far above what things are worth. In the Dutch Republic in the 1630s, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared, and then they crashed in early 1637.

Modern historians have found, however, that the tulip story was probably exaggerated. Few people seem to have been ruined, and the famous tale comes mostly from writers who wanted to warn against greed.

In 1720, shares in the British South Sea Company rose to many times their old price, and then fell sharply. Thousands of investors lost money, and the famous scientist Isaac Newton is said to have been one of them.
In nearly every bubble, people say that this time is different, and that old rules no longer apply. Fear of missing out then pushes them to join in, long after prices have stopped making sense.
Rule five is that hunger and public anger can bring down even a strong government. In France, the harvest of 1788 was poor, so bread became very expensive in 1789.
In May 1789, the king called an assembly to deal with the debts. On 14 July, a crowd in Paris attacked the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison, and the revolution began.
Some historians argue that revolutions rarely begin when people are at their very poorest. They more often come when hopes have risen and are then suddenly disappointed, as happened in France.
The French Revolution did not end in freedom for all. In 1799, a successful general named Napoleon took power, and in 1804 he crowned himself emperor.
Rule six is that sudden disasters can change who holds power. In 1347, ships carrying sick sailors reached Sicily from the Black Sea, and the Black Death came to Europe.
Nobody knows exactly how many people died in the Black Death. Most historians think that perhaps a third or more of Europe's people died in about four years.

With so many workers dead, those who survived could ask for higher wages, and some moved to find better pay. In 1351, England passed a law trying to freeze wages at their old level, but it was widely ignored.
In 1381, anger over a new tax and old rules led to the Peasants' Revolt in England. The rebels were defeated, but over the next century the old system of serfdom slowly faded in England.
Rule seven is that history is often written by the winners. Most old records were made by people who served kings, priests and governments, so they show the world as the powerful saw it.
In 146 BC, Rome destroyed the city of Carthage, its great rival across the sea. Much of what we know about Carthage was written by Greeks and Romans, who were its enemies.
A good reader of history asks who wrote a text, for whom, and why. It also helps to look for other kinds of evidence, such as letters, diaries, objects and the remains of buildings.
Rule eight is that the way a war ends shapes the peace that follows. After Napoleon was defeated, the great powers met at the Congress of Vienna in 1814 and 1815.

After the First World War, the Treaty of Versailles took land from Germany, limited its army and demanded reparations. Many Germans felt that it was unfair and humiliating, and later politicians used that anger.
Peace tends to last longer when the losers feel that they still have a place in the world. It is not the only cause of what happens next, because economies, leaders and chance also matter.

Rule nine is that great powers usually decline slowly, and then seem to collapse quickly. In 476, a general named Odoacer removed the last Roman emperor in the West, a teenager called Romulus Augustulus.

In truth, Rome had been under strain for more than two hundred years, with civil wars, plague, invasions and money troubles. The eastern half of the empire survived, and its capital, Constantinople, did not fall until 1453.
Collapse looks sudden in the books, but it is built slowly, through small failures that people get used to. Those who live through it often cannot tell that an age is ending.
Rule ten is that places where people, goods and ideas meet tend to grow rich. Venice, a city built on islands in a lagoon, became a great power by trading between Europe and the East.

For well over a thousand years, the trade routes known as the Silk Road joined China with the Mediterranean. They carried silk, spices and metals, and also religions, inventions and, sometimes, disease.
In 1498, the Portuguese sailor Vasco da Gama reached India by sailing around Africa. Over time, trade moved towards Atlantic ports such as Lisbon, and Venice lost some of its old advantage.

Rule eleven is that reform comes in waves, and each wave meets resistance. British campaigners worked for decades to end the slave trade, banned in 1807, and then slavery itself, abolished by law in 1833.

In 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the right to vote in national elections. Other countries followed slowly, and in some places women waited until well into the twentieth century.

Progress is rarely a straight line, because reform and reaction tend to follow each other like waves. Rights that were won can be lost again, so each generation has to defend what earlier ones achieved.
Rule twelve is that leaders often prepare for the last war instead of the next one. After the First World War, France built the Maginot Line, a chain of strong forts along its border with Germany.

Human memory is short, and when the people who lived through a war or a disaster have died, its lessons tend to fade. Younger generations, who have never felt the danger, may then repeat the old mistakes.
This is one reason that history is taught, written and kept in libraries. A history book is a kind of shared memory that lets us borrow experience without paying its price.
Even so, chance and personal choice always play a part in history. A storm, an illness or a single decision can turn events in a way that nobody expected.
When you study any event, you can ask three simple questions. Who gains from it, who pays for it, and what do the people involved believe?
The best way to use a pattern is to compare, not to copy. Ask what is the same today, and then ask carefully what is different.
Historians often disagree, and they change their minds when new evidence is found. This is not a weakness, because it shows that the study of the past is still alive.
History never repeats itself exactly, but it often rhymes. If you learn these patterns and test them against the facts, you will see the world with clearer eyes.
C1C2: People often say that history repeats itself, but no event has ever happened in exactly the same way twice. What returns, in different clothes and in different centuries, is a pattern: a habit of people and societies that shows itself whenever the conditions are right. This book follows twelve of those patterns, each one seen through real examples from across the world.

Tools, clothes and languages change from one century to the next, but the needs of people stay surprisingly steady. In every age, they have wanted food, safety, respect and a better life for their children, and they have feared losing these things. It is these steady wants and fears that make patterns appear in history, even among societies that never met.

A pattern in history is a tendency, not a law of nature like gravity, and it can always be broken by people who see it coming. One example proves nothing, and a pattern is only worth trusting when it appears in many places and times. Throughout this book, the examples are chosen to show a habit at work, and the exceptions are mentioned where they matter.

The first rule is that empires tend to grow larger than they can comfortably guard. Around the year 117, under the Emperor Trajan, the Roman Empire reached its greatest size, stretching from Britain in the north-west to Mesopotamia in the east. Within a few years, however, his successor Hadrian gave up some of the newest conquests in the east, judging that they were not worth the cost of holding.

A long frontier needs soldiers, and soldiers need food, clothing, weapons and regular pay, all carried across great distances along roads and rivers. The Roman army was paid chiefly in silver coins, so that every new border and every new campaign made the emperor's bills larger. In many places and at many times, the lands that were guarded cost more to hold than they gave back in taxes, and the empire felt the strain.

In the 1500s, Spain ruled huge territories on several continents, and silver from its mines in the Americas poured into its treasury. Even so, the cost of fighting wars across Europe and defending distant shipping lanes was so great that the Spanish crown declared itself unable to pay its debts several times between the 1550s and the 1640s. Wealth that had looked endless had in fact been spent faster than it arrived, and the treasury was empty again.

Leaders rarely give up distant lands willingly, because retreat feels like defeat, and defeat can threaten their own position at home. Empires therefore tend to keep spending on a frontier long after it has stopped paying for itself, and the wise ruler who pulls back in time is the exception. That is the first rule: power spreads until its cost exceeds its strength, and then it must either shrink or break.

The second rule is that tricks with money, however clever they seem at first, nearly always end badly. Roman emperors who struggled to pay their armies found a tempting answer: they mixed cheaper metals into the silver of their coins, so that the same amount of silver could be made into more of them. Each change was small, but over the decades the silver in the coin dwindled until, by the middle of the third century, little of it was left.

Merchants and farmers soon noticed that the coins were worth less than before, so they asked for more of them, and prices climbed. In the year 301, the emperor Diocletian tried to stop the rise by issuing an edict that fixed the highest prices for hundreds of goods. Historians generally agree that it failed, for according to some writers of the time, goods simply vanished from the markets.

In Germany in 1923, prices rose so fast that workers were paid every day and hurried to spend their pay, and bundles of banknotes were carried in bags and wheelbarrows. By November, a single American dollar was worth about four trillion German marks, and the savings of ordinary families had become almost worthless. The government had been printing money to pay its bills, and the more it printed, the less each note was worth.

Money is really a shared belief, and it works only as long as people expect it to keep its value. In November 1923, Germany introduced a new currency, the Rentenmark, and together with other reforms it helped to bring the rise in prices to an end. The lesson, repeated in many countries and centuries, is that trust takes years to build and only a short time to destroy.

The third rule is that every new way of sharing information shakes the people who hold power. Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press with moveable metal letters in the German city of Mainz, and books, which had once been copied slowly by hand, began to be made in quantity. Within a lifetime, printers had set up shops in a great many towns across Europe.

In 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther wrote a list of arguments against certain practices of the Church, known as the Ninety-five Theses. Printers soon copied his writings and sold them in towns across Germany, so that his ideas spread far faster than any scribe could have carried them. The Church and the princes found that they could no longer control what people read, and a religious movement, the Reformation, grew from this.

In 1844, the first long-distance message by electric telegraph was sent in the United States, between Washington and Baltimore. A first cable under the Atlantic worked briefly in 1858 and a lasting one was laid in 1866, and news that had once needed days to cross the ocean began to arrive in minutes. Governments, bankers and newspapers all had to learn to act in a world where events were known almost instantly.

Each time, those in power tried to take control of the new tool: in 1559, for example, the Catholic Church issued a list of banned books, and many rulers licensed their printers and censored the news. Yet each new tool carried rumour, propaganda and lies as well as knowledge, and it took societies years, sometimes generations, to learn how to use it wisely. That is the third rule: every new way to share information disturbs the old order, helps some and harms others, and is never simply good or bad.

The fourth rule is that crowds can push prices far above what things are truly worth, until the day the buying stops. In the Dutch Republic in the 1630s, the price of rare tulip bulbs, especially those with striped patterns, soared to levels that pamphlets of the time claimed were worth a fine house, and then crashed in early 1637. People bought not because they loved flowers but because they expected someone else to pay more tomorrow.

Modern historians have found, however, that the tulip story has probably been exaggerated in the retelling. The records show that a good many contracts were never honoured, but few people seem to have been ruined, and much of the famous tale comes from writers who wanted to warn readers against greed. It is a useful reminder that even a famous example should be checked, which is itself a rule worth following.

In 1720, shares in the British South Sea Company, which claimed a trade monopoly in South America, rose to roughly eight times their January price before collapsing within months. Thousands of investors were ruined, and the great scientist Isaac Newton is said to have lost a large sum of money. Parliament investigated the affair, and several people connected with the company were punished for their part in it.

In nearly every bubble, people tell one another that this time is different, that the old rules of value no longer apply, and that those who doubt are simply behind the times. Fear of missing out then pulls even careful people into the crowd, long after prices have stopped making any sense. The fourth rule is that when a price climbs because others are buying, and not because of what the thing is worth, a fall is coming, though nobody can say exactly when.

The fifth rule is that hunger and public anger can bring down even a strong government. In France, the harvest of 1788 was poor, and by the spring of 1789 the price of bread had risen so high that ordinary families spent a large part of their wages on it. At the same time the royal government, burdened by debts from earlier wars, was struggling to find money.

In May 1789, King Louis XVI called a great assembly of the whole country, the Estates-General, to deal with the crisis. Within weeks the assembly had turned into a challenge to the king himself, and on 14 July a Paris crowd, searching for gunpowder and weapons, stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress that served as a prison. The revolution that followed would change France, and the memory of it would shape the politics of many other countries.

Some historians argue that revolutions rarely begin when people are at their very poorest, for the poorest are usually too busy surviving to rebel. They more often come when conditions have been improving, hopes have risen, and then a bad harvest, a lost war or an unfair tax makes people feel cheated. This idea, first put forward in the nineteenth century by the French writer Alexis de Tocqueville, does not fit every case, but it has helped to explain many of them.

The French Revolution began with demands for liberty and equality, but it passed through years of violence and fear and did not end in a lasting republic. In 1799, a successful young general named Napoleon Bonaparte seized power, and in 1804 he crowned himself emperor. Many people accepted him because he promised order, and so the fifth rule carries a warning: after great upheavals, exhausted societies often welcome a strong ruler who offers calm.

The sixth rule is that sudden disasters can change who holds power, long after the disaster itself has ended. In October 1347, trading ships from the Black Sea reached the Sicilian port of Messina with sick and dying sailors aboard, and the Black Death, a plague spread chiefly by fleas, began to move across Europe. Within four years it had reached nearly every part of the continent, and almost no family was left untouched by it.

Nobody knows exactly how many people died in the Black Death, because records were poor and many of those who kept them also died. Most historians now think that perhaps a third or more of Europe's people were lost within about four years, though some regions suffered far more and others far less. Whole villages emptied, fields lay unploughed, and those who survived had to find a way to carry on.

With so many workers dead, those who survived suddenly found their labour in demand, and they asked for higher wages or moved to estates where the pay was better. Landowners, who had grown used to cheap labour, were alarmed, and in 1351 the English Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers, which tried to freeze wages at their old level. The law was widely ignored, because a worker who was refused fair pay could always find another employer who needed hands.

In 1381, anger over a new tax, together with resentment of the old rules that tied workers to the land, led to the Peasants' Revolt in England. The rebel leaders were defeated, and many were executed, yet over the following century the old system of serfdom slowly faded away. The sixth rule shows itself here: when a shock suddenly changes who is scarce and who is not, the balance of power between rich and poor shifts, whatever the law may say.

The seventh rule is that history is usually written by the winners, or at least by those who held power when the writing was done. Most old records were made by scribes and officials who served kings, priests and governments, and they naturally preserved the stories that favoured their masters. Ordinary farmers, women, slaves and defeated peoples left far fewer words behind, and so their lives must often be pieced together from other clues.

In 146 BC, after three long wars, Rome destroyed the city of Carthage, its great rival across the Mediterranean Sea, and most of the Carthaginians' own writings were lost. Much of what we know about them was therefore written by Greeks and Romans, who were their enemies or their conquerors. Archaeologists have since dug up houses, harbours and burial grounds that give a fuller and sometimes different picture.

A careful reader of history therefore asks who wrote each text, for whom, and why, and what the writer might have wished to hide. It also helps to look for other kinds of evidence, such as private letters, diaries, tax records, objects and the remains of buildings, which were often made without any thought of impressing posterity. The seventh rule teaches patience and doubt: the first story we are told is rarely the whole one.

The eighth rule is that the way a war ends shapes the peace that follows it. When Napoleon was finally defeated, the great powers met at the Congress of Vienna in 1814 and 1815, and they chose to treat France firmly but not to crush it, so that it kept its place among the leading nations. The result was a long period without a war that drew in every great power, though smaller wars and revolutions did not stop.

After the First World War, the Treaty of Versailles of 1919 took land from Germany, limited its army and demanded large payments, called reparations, for the damage of the war. Many Germans felt that it was unfair and humiliating, and in the following years ambitious politicians learned to use that anger. Historians still debate whether the treaty was too harsh, or not enforced firmly enough, and how large a part it played in the next war.

Peace tends to last longer when the defeated feel that they still have a place in the new order and a chance to recover. It would be wrong to blame one treaty for everything that came after it, because economic crises, ambitious leaders and sheer chance all played their parts. What the eighth rule says is that the ending of a war plants seeds, and people will harvest them for generations.

The ninth rule is that great powers usually decline slowly, and then appear to collapse almost overnight. In the year 476, a general named Odoacer removed Romulus Augustulus, a teenage boy who was the last Roman emperor in the West, and sent him into comfortable retirement. Later writers chose that date as the end of the Western Roman Empire, though few who lived through it can have thought that an age had ended.

In truth, the Western Empire had been under strain for more than two centuries, struggling with civil wars, plagues, invasions, weak emperors and a currency that nobody trusted. Its Eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, was richer and better defended, and it survived for almost a thousand years more, until the city fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Rome's story shows that empires rarely end on a single day, whatever the textbook date says.

To the people who lived through the long decline, most days looked like any other, and each small failure was explained away as something temporary. Roads were mended less often, taxes were collected less fairly, and armies were filled with soldiers who felt less loyalty to the state. The ninth rule is a warning that collapse, when it seems sudden, has usually been prepared by many years of small neglect.

The tenth rule is that places where people, goods and ideas meet tend to grow wealthy and inventive. Venice, a city built on islands in a shallow lagoon with almost no farmland of its own, became one of the richest places in Europe by trading between the Mediterranean and the East. For roughly a thousand years, until 1797, it remained an independent republic, and its shipyard, the Arsenal, was famous for building ships with remarkable speed.

For well over a thousand years, a web of trade routes later called the Silk Road linked China with India, Persia and the Mediterranean. Along it travelled silk, spices, metals and horses, and with them went religions, inventions such as paper-making and, sometimes, deadly diseases. Towns along the way, such as Samarkand and Kashgar, grew rich by feeding, housing and taxing the merchants who passed through.

In 1498, the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama reached India by sailing around the southern tip of Africa, and a new sea route opened between Europe and Asia. Over the following decades, much of the spice trade moved towards ports facing the Atlantic, such as Lisbon and later Amsterdam, and Venice lost some of its old advantage. The tenth rule has a second half: when the routes change, the wealth that depended on them moves too.

The eleventh rule is that reform comes in waves, and that every wave meets resistance from those who gain by the old way. In Britain, campaigners worked for decades, through petitions, speeches, boycotts and the testimony of those who had been enslaved, to end the slave trade, which Parliament banned in 1807. Slavery itself was abolished throughout most of the empire by an act of 1833, yet former owners received huge payments from the government, while the people they had enslaved received nothing.

In 1893, after years of petitions signed by tens of thousands of New Zealanders, the country became the first self-governing nation to give women the right to vote in national elections. Other countries followed only slowly, and in some of them, such as Switzerland, women could not vote in national elections until 1971. Each advance was won by campaigners who had been assured, year after year, that the moment was not yet ripe.

Progress is rarely a straight line, for reform and reaction tend to follow each other like the tide coming in and going out. Rights that were won through years of struggle can be narrowed or removed again, and ideas once thought dead can return in new clothes. The eleventh rule is therefore a reminder that every generation inherits its freedoms as a trust, and must work to keep them.

The twelfth rule is that leaders and generals tend to prepare for the last war and not the next one. After the terrible trench fighting of the First World War, France spent the 1930s building a chain of strong forts, the Maginot Line, along its border with Germany. In May 1940, however, German tanks advanced through the forested hills of the Ardennes, which French planners had considered too difficult to cross, and France was defeated in about six weeks.

Human memory is short, and when the last people who lived through a war, a famine or a financial crash have died, the lessons they carried tend to die with them. Younger generations, who have never felt the danger, may then regard the old warnings as exaggerated or even as boring. It is not that people are foolish, but that experience cannot be inherited in the way that money can.

That is one reason why history is taught in schools, written in books and kept safe in archives and libraries. A good history works as a kind of shared memory, lending us the experience of people who paid dearly for it, so that we may learn without paying the same price. It cannot make us wise by itself, but it can make us a good deal less surprised by what the world does next.

Even so, chance and personal choice always play a part, and no pattern can tell us exactly what will happen. A storm, an illness, an accident or a single brave or foolish decision can turn events in a direction that nobody expected. The rules in this book describe what is likely, not what is certain, in the way that a weather forecast speaks of rain without promising it.

When you study any event, past or present, you can ask three simple questions that open most doors. Who gains from what is happening, who pays for it, and what do the people involved believe about the world? Answers to these questions, taken together, explain a surprising number of the turning points in this book.

The best way to use any pattern from the past is to compare it with the present and not simply to copy it. Ask what is the same in the situation you are studying, and then ask, just as carefully, what is different, for the differences are often where the real surprises lie. Technology, population, climate and ideas all change, so an old lesson must always be tested against new facts before it is trusted.

Historians often disagree with one another, and they change their minds when new evidence comes to light, such as a newly opened archive, a better dating method or a buried city. This is not a weakness of the subject but a sign that it is alive, for a history that never changed would be one that nobody was checking. The humble reader holds every rule loosely, remains ready to be corrected, and treats each new discovery as a gift rather than a threat.

History never repeats itself exactly, but it often rhymes, and the patterns in this book are its most familiar rhymes. Empires stretch too far, money tricks fail, crowds chase bubbles, disasters shift power and reformers meet resistance, while the stories we are told are shaped by those who tell them. Knowing these habits will not let us predict the future, but it can help us face it with open eyes, steady nerves and a little more wisdom.
